title: App Store vs. web pricing: what changes when you move to the web
summary: Compare App Store vs. web pricing: the price changes, trials, offers, and payment methods you gain, and the refunds, disputes, and tax you take on.
body_markdown:
Pricing on the web vs. the App Store(s) is a lot like making the shift from agency to freelancer. When I speak with people at agencies, they often envy the freelance life — they imagine no agency cut and complete freedom. It sounds dreamy.


What they don’t realize (and what I didn’t realize at the beginning) is that the extra cut doesn’t go directly into your pocket. It pays for your accountant, software, a pension scheme, legal insurance, tooling... The extra freedom of freelance comes with extra costs and extra jobs.


[Pricing on the App Store](https://www.revenuecat.com/blog/engineering/app-store-fees) is similar. You think, “Yes, I can avoid that up-to-30% cut,” only to learn the hard way what Apple was actually doing for you behind the scenes, from handling taxes and refunds, to navigating global legislation.


Yes,[web-to-app](https://www.revenuecat.com/blog/growth/web-to-app-funnels) is a huge opportunity. But it comes with different pricing systems, different freedoms, and different jobs. The 30% is the least interesting part of it.


If you’re considering moving to the web, or are just starting to explore it, this is everything you need to know about pricing on the[web versus pricing in-app](https://www.revenuecat.com/blog/growth/iap-vs-web-purchases-conversion-test) .


## App Store vs. web pricing: full comparison overview


I want to help you understand what Apple, the “agency,” was quietly doing for you behind the scenes, and what the app stores also lock you into. I’ve never seen this laid out in one place, so here’s the full overview for you to bookmark and refer back to.


TL;DR


Web pricing is more flexible, offering freedom when it comes to price testing and experimentation, but it also comes with new complexities — and a new set of regulations.


Pricing move


On the app stores


On the web


What you need to manage

Consent screen above ~$5 / $50 or 50%, once a year; no opt-in means expiry

Every existing subscriber gets it, and it can't be reversed


A code, a cohort or a time window


Codes don't stack with intro offers


Test a price


New product in a group every subscriber can browse

Saved prices can't be edited; name products for the long run


Set a trial


3 days to 1 year, fixed steps, one per group per customer


Any length, any first-period price


Visa's trial rules, card testing, your own dunning

Apple Pay, cards, HSA/FSA, Pix, iDEAL


Disputes: Visa 1.5%, Mastercard 1.5% + 100

Your own index


Keeping it current


## 5 Things the app stores never let you do


Before we can dive into what you can do differently with web pricing, it's worth mapping out what the restrictions are in the app stores. Some of these are mildly annoying, like Apple's price grid, while others like subscription group visibility, have no workaround.


### 1. Raise your price without asking permission


When you increase the price of an iOS subscription beyond a threshold set by Apple, Apple sends every subscriber an option to agree to the new price. If they don’t opt in, their subscription ends at the end of the current billing cycle.


At the time of writing,[the rules](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/advancedcommerceapi/handling-subscription-price-changes) are:


- The increase is more than 50% of the current price, **and**
- The dollar increase is more than:


- **$5 per billing period** for non-annual subscriptions
- **$50 per year** for annual subscriptions


There are some additional restrictions, too. You can only increase the price once every 12 months, and Apple also considers whether the local market requires explicit consent.


Austria and Germany are notable exceptions: in these countries, you’re required to get subscriber consent for **any** price increase.


If a subscriber doesn’t consent, the subscription expires at the end of their current billing cycle.


Credit: TechCrunch


The Play Store is even stricter. Opt-in is the default in every region, with 37 days’ notice required for a price increase. Price decreases, on the other hand, don’t require consent.


Weightloss app,[Lose It!](https://www.loseit.com/) , was so unimpressed with Apple’s flow that they chose not to implement a price increase for existing customers when they doubled their annual price from $40 to $80. Patrick Rills, their Chief Product & Technology Officer at the time, shared their reasoning on a[Sub Club episode](https://subclub.com/episode/the-hidden-cost-of-underpricing-your-subscription-patrick-rills-lose-it) :


“The way that you have to increase the price on existing subscriptions in the app store, I feel like the UX is confusing and cumbersome… To us, it was impossible to A/B test. It was a huge risk for us that we felt like we couldn't take on.”


On the web, the process is much simpler: announce the price increase, choose a date, and implement it. Lose It! could have raised prices for existing subscribers gradually, by cohort, rather than having to move everyone through the same consent flow.


The Apple App Store’s consent flow is clumsy at best, but it does force some discipline around larger price increases. The web offers far more flexibility, but that flexibility can also make it easier to get price increases badly wrong. I’ve seen some pretty shocking[price increase communications](https://www.revenuecat.com/blog/growth/how-to-raise-app-prices-effectively) .


Regulation is also starting to close some of that gap. Since November 2025, New York has required either consent or a 14-day refund window for certain subscription price increases, rather than allowing businesses to simply notify customers. Around 30 US states also now have laws governing auto-renewing subscriptions.


The result is an important distinction: moving pricing to the web gives you much more control, but it also means taking on much more responsibility for how and when you use that control.


### 2. Casually decrease your price


Price increases aren’t the only pricing changes with rules. Imagine you’ve been testing pricing with your new subscribers, and now it’s time to tidy things up.


When Lose It! was testing prices, they went as high as $120 per year before settling on $80. Luckily, they caught it during testing. But sometimes you only discover retrospectively, once the retention data comes through, that maybe the old price was better.


So you decide to reverse course. Easy, right? Just decrease the price for future subscribers.


Here’s the catch: on both the App Store and Google Play, a price decrease doesn’t just apply to new subscribers. **Existing subscribers are moved to the lower price, too.** And once you implement that decrease, you can’t reverse it.


With a price increase, at least you can choose to apply it only to new subscribers. That means decreasing your price comes with a much higher cost: you’re not just changing your future pricing, you’re potentially changing the economics of your entire existing subscriber base.


On the web, this is much simpler. You can lower the price for a new cohort without affecting everyone who came before them. You have the flexibility to charge different customers different prices at different times.


One thing worth knowing if you’re using[RevenueCat Web Billing](https://www.revenuecat.com/blog/company/flexible-discounts-web-billing) : you can’t edit a saved price in an existing currency; you need to create a new product instead. That means if you adjust your pricing often, you can end up with a messy subscription-group graveyard.


Luckily, on the web, you’re the only one who sees that mess. Think of it like shutting the tupperware cupboard — you know it’s chaos inside, but no one else does.


### 3. Test pricing without your subscribers watching


Talking of pricing changes… unlike the web’s messy proverbial cupboard, on the Apple App Store the history of price changes is much more visible.


I know when an app has been price testing, because I go to their subscriptions and can see all the different prices and options they've tested over time. I try to behave, but sometimes it is hard to resist switching to a lower tier that I see there.


One app's subscription list after a few years of testing. Count the duplicates. Every subscriber can find this screen in their settings.


That’s not a bug; it’s how subscription groups work. Every product you’ve ever put in a subscription group sits under **Manage Subscription** , and Apple lets customers upgrade, downgrade, and crossgrade between them. So that price you tested back in 2023? Yep, it’s still there.


Compare that with the web, where a price change can be represented by a URL parameter, product ID, or coupon rather than creating a new SKU that sits in a subscription group for all your subscribers to browse.


The mess is still there. It’s just hidden in the cupboard. It’s like that episode of *Friends* where you find out Monica has a hidden chaos cupboard.


And pricing history isn’t the only thing the app stores lock down. There are several other decisions they make for you that the web leaves open:


- **Trial length:** Apple gives you a fixed list of options: 3 days, 1 or 2 weeks, 1, 2, 3, or 6 months, or a year. You can also only have one[introductory offer](https://www.revenuecat.com/blog/company/introductory-offers-for-revenuecat-web-billing) per subscription group per customer. On the web, you can choose any number of days you want.
- **Plan structure:** the app stores structure plans around weeks, months, and years. Some apps using web funnels instead prefer to sell based on an outcome or commitment length, for example, a 12-week plan, which you can’t offer natively in the same way on the app stores.


For most apps, these limitations won’t make much difference. But for some, having control over the length and structure of a plan can be important, and those alternatives simply aren’t available in-app.


Take[YNAB, a financial planning app](https://www.revenuecat.com/blog/growth/web-to-app-funnel-examples) . Through its web funnel, YNAB offers a[34-day free trial](https://www.revenuecat.com/blog/growth/7-day-trial-subscription-app) . That would never be possible on the app stores. But for a budgeting app, that extra time can make a real difference: you get over a month to see paycheck-to-paycheck whether your spending habits are changing.


So if you feel that there's more to gain in terms of pricing, it may be better to run these experiments on the web, where the traces of your experiments won't follow you, and you have the flexibility to test them as you like. Whether that's:


- An alternative[trial length](https://www.revenuecat.com/blog/growth/7-day-trial-subscription-app)
- Testing an increase or decrease in price
- Setting up your plans around the outcome length instead of the calendar


### 4. Use structures that do not exist for in-app purchases (IAPs)


So far this has been about prices you already have. But the web also lets you sell shapes that don't exist for in-app purchases at all.


#### A. Paid trials


A paid trial[filters for intent and sends the ad platforms a buyer,](https://www.revenuecat.com/blog/growth/free-trials-dont-make-sense-anymore) not a browser.[Apple's pay-up-front intro offers](https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/manage-subscriptions/set-up-introductory-offers-for-auto-renewable-subscriptions) are similar, but each customer can redeem one per subscription group. On the web, the first-period price is whatever you want it to be.


This is also key, as it allows you to test different paid trial lengths and price points. It can be quite a balance to get right. Too cheap, and you devalue the product afterward. Too expensive, and while your ARPPU may increase, you'll see a drop in volume.


It can also help you combat fake card information online, since they'll need at least the paid trial amount on their card.


#### B. Money-back guarantees


These kinds of guarantees really only work properly on the web, where the refund button is one you actually control. That gives you the ability to make a genuine guarantee, and it can also help you attract higher-quality customers.


[Reading.com](http://reading.com/) swapped its web free trial for a 30-day[money-back guarantee](https://www.revenuecat.com/blog/growth/money-back-guarantee) with upfront payment. Conversion rate dropped, but revenue and LTV increased, so they decided to keep the model for certain funnels. Tim Dikun also shared that barely anyone actually asked for a refund.


You could add a money-back guarantee to an app, and I’ve seen a few apps do it. But there’s a fundamental problem: the refund is ultimately in the hands of the app store.


You’re therefore promising something you don’t fully control.


On the web, the guarantee is yours to define, deliver, and optimize. Just another small example of how moving the transaction off the store gives you more than just control over pricing; you gain control over the entire commercial experience.


#### C. Upsells and add-ons after purchase


Cristian Rotari shared at Appsforum London 2026 that, in his experience, upgrades — such as moving customers from monthly to annual plans — can generate around 20–30% in additional revenue, while add-ons can contribute up to 40% on yearly plans.


For example,[Teaching.com offers $9.99 printables](https://subclub.com/episode/what-readingcom-learned-testing-prices-and-funnels-tim-dikun-teachingcom) , which around 20% of customers purchase. Noom, meanwhile, runs six upsells and two upgrade options.


This kind of monetization is much harder to implement in the app stores. And if your add-on is a[physical product](https://www.revenuecat.com/blog/growth/combining-subscriptions-physical-products) , you can’t sell it directly through an app store subscription at all.


On the web, you can build your subscription around the core product, then layer on any additional offers that make sense: upgrades, add-ons, physical products, or entirely separate purchases.


#### D. Payment methods


There are also payment options that Apple doesn’t natively support, and they’re much easier to offer at[web checkout](https://www.revenuecat.com/blog/growth/why-you-shouldnt-use-app-to-web) .


One example is HSA/FSA payments in the US, which let eligible customers use pre-tax health savings or flexible spending account funds to pay for qualifying health and wellness products. For some apps, this can make a meaningful difference at checkout.[Truemed claims](https://www.truemed.com/partners) that offering HSA/FSA eligibility led to a 22% increase in average order value (AOV) and a 10% average lift in checkout conversion. Major health and fitness apps are starting to offer this option too, including Calm, Peloton, and MyFitnessPal.


Gift subscriptions are another example: the app stores supports offer codes, but they don’t provide quite the same gifting experience. On the web, Headspace has a dedicated gift page where customers can choose a plan, add a personal message, and even schedule when the gift will be sent.


Then there are local payment methods. With a payment provider like Stripe, you can offer Pix in Brazil, UPI in India, and iDEAL in the Netherlands. These aren’t just nice-to-have alternatives. In some markets, they’re the default payment methods people know and trust, making them a much more natural way to pay.


Many times I’ve traveled with friends from the Netherlands and watched them get completely stuck trying to pay for something abroad because iDEAL wasn’t available. Credit cards simply aren’t as widely used there. Offering the payment method people already rely on can make the difference between a completed purchase and an abandoned checkout.


### 5. Set a price that isn’t in the pricing grid


This one falls firmly into the ‘mildly annoying’ category, but it’s worth mentioning because of its impact on international pricing.


Behind every App Store price is a grid. Apple offers up to 900 price points, with 800 available by default. The top 100, covering roughly $1,000 and above, require an Account Holder request. It used to be much worse: until December 2022, there were only around 100 price points. Today, prices move in $0.10 increments up to $10 and $0.50 increments between $10 and $50, with prices anchored to .99. So $47.99 exists, but $47.97 doesn’t.


Honestly, this is a bit like complaining in a candy shop that they stock hundreds of sweets but not your exact favorite. Just pick one of the other 800. For the price itself, that’s fair enough.


The real catch is what happens across your other markets. When you set a subscription price in App Store Connect, Apple suggests equivalent prices for the other 174 storefronts based on current exchange rates and applicable taxes. Then those prices largely stay put. Apple periodically adjusts prices for currency fluctuations, but these adjustments explicitly exclude auto-renewable subscriptions.


So if the pound moves 15% against the dollar, your UK subscription price won’t automatically follow suit. Regional prices can quietly drift out of sync with exchange rates, purchasing power, and what customers in each market are willing to pay.


[Regional pricing is a huge opportunity](https://www.revenuecat.com/blog/growth/price-localization-for-apps) , and it’s much easier to experiment with on the web. Take Simply, the company behind Simply Piano, Simply Guitar, Simply Sing, Simply Draw, and Simply Tune. It went as far as building its own purchasing-power index.[Yoav Sharon, its Head of Growth and Product, shared on Sub Club](https://subclub.com/episode/how-simply-finally-cracked-facebook-ads-with-web-funnels-yoav-sharon-simply) that the company now generates around 20% of its revenue through web campaigns, a channel where its app-only ads had previously flopped.


## 4 Things the app stores help with


So, we’ve had a good old rant about app stores, but in fairness, it’s time to hear their side of the story. Just as my husband insists on playing Devil’s Advocate whenever someone has wronged me, I’ll step up and defend the app stores for a moment.


Because, as I hinted at in the opening, app stores have been quietly taking care of a lot of things for you. And when you move pricing to the web, those responsibilities don’t disappear. They become yours.


Remember the accountant and the pension scheme from the opening? Let’s look at what the app stores have been quietly handling behind the scenes.


### 1. Deal with messy and high refunds


A quick caveat: in-app refunds can be high, but for most apps I’ve seen, unless they’re doing something a little cheeky in the grey zone, refund rates typically fall between 2% and 5%. That tracks with the broader data: median refund rates across categories range from 2.5% to 4.7%, with Photo & Video, Productivity, and Business standing out as categories with higher rates.


I couldn’t find reliable data on refund rates for web funnels specifically for apps. In my experience, though, they tend to be a little higher — around 5–6% — especially if you start experimenting with upsells or offer a money-back guarantee.


On the App Store for example, you don’t process refunds. Apple does. Your involvement is usually limited to a 12-hour window to submit supporting information if Apple requests it. Apple handles the rest. You might need to weigh in on some cases, but overall, it’s not much hassle.


With web subscriptions, you set the refund policy and manage the process yourself. That means you need to **process refunds quickly and generously** , because otherwise, they can turn into disputes — another messy part of running payments on the web.


A refused $30 refund can become a $30 dispute, plus $15 in dispute fees, and it counts against your dispute rate. In other words, refusing a refund can end up costing you more than simply granting it.


### 2. Deal with disputes


If a user disputes a charge, you’ll need to either provide evidence that the charge was legitimate or accept the dispute. Either way, it can cost you in several ways:


1. **Dispute fee:** for example,[Stripe charges $15 (or €20 in Europe) per dispute, plus another $15 (or €20 in Europe) if you choose to challenge it](https://www.chargeback.io/blog/stripe-chargeback-rate) .
2. **Card network thresholds:** most card networks have thresholds for dispute rates, and exceeding them can trigger monitoring programs and penalties. For example, Mastercard’s Excessive Chargeback Merchant (ECM) program has historically used a threshold of 1.5% and at least 100 chargebacks per month. Penalties can escalate over time, reaching as much as $100,000 per month by month 19. In other words, this isn’t something to take lightly.


There are tools that can help you manage disputes, but prevention is the better strategy. Make sure your payment terms and billing descriptors are clear, notify users about upcoming and recurring charges, and make it easy for them to cancel subscriptions or manage their accounts.


Avoid dark patterns that leave customers feeling misled or trapped. The fewer unpleasant surprises your billing creates, the fewer disputes you’re likely to face.


### 3. Deal with failed cards and free trial challenges


Both Apple and Google handle billing retries, but even then,[15.2% (App Store) to 32.2% (Play) of cancellations are still billing errors.](https://www.revenuecat.com/state-of-subscription-apps/)


On the web, this can be even more challenging because some users rely on virtual or disposable cards specifically to avoid recurring subscription charges. When those payments fail, you have to deal with the fallout yourself. In the App Store, Apple’s billing system handles much of this for you.


Fortunately, there are tools to help reduce failed payments and recover revenue. Stripe, for example, offers Smart Retries and dunning emails to recover failed payments. Stripe[claims a recovery rate of around 55%](https://stripe.com/gb/billing) across its customer base, although[Redux Payments, analysing more than 200 Stripe accounts](https://www.reduxpayments.com/blog/stripe-smart-retries-explained) , found the figure was closer to 25–35%.


All of this adds friction to running subscriptions on the web. Free trials are a good example. Visa’s[2020 subscription trial rules](https://usa.visa.com/dam/VCOM/global/support-legal/documents/visa-new-subscription-rules-flier.pdf) , for instance, require a reminder at least seven days before the first charge, express customer consent, an easy way to cancel online, and a statement descriptor that identifies the trial. Miss these requirements, and that first post-trial charge can quickly become a dispute.


As a result, free trials can be harder to run effectively on the web. We’re seeing more apps experiment with the alternatives discussed earlier, from paid trials to money-back guarantees.


If you do decide to offer a free trial on the web, make sure your reminder and dunning emails are set up properly. They can help prevent surprises, recover failed payments, and reduce avoidable disputes.


### 4. Dealing with different laws


I’ve bundled these together because I know dealing with legislation is everyone’s least favorite part of running a business. But when you move subscriptions to the web, there are two areas you need to pay particular attention to.


#### A. Tax laws


The app stores handle much of the complexity around taxes and local regulations across different markets. If you sell subscriptions in multiple countries, that’s no small thing.


On the web, you’re responsible for getting this right yourself. There are solutions, such as Merchant of Record services like[Paddle](https://www.revenuecat.com/integrations/revenuecat-paddle) and[Stripe Managed Payments](https://www.revenuecat.com/blog/company/stripe-managed-payments-revenuecat-web) , that can take much of this burden off your shoulders. But they come at an additional cost and introduce another layer to your setup.


#### B. Cancellation laws


The other area you need to research carefully is the legislation governing subscription cancellations. Requirements vary by country, including how you present cancellation options and how easy you make it for customers to cancel.


For example, Germany requires a cancellation button for certain online consumer contracts, while France has specific requirements for making online cancellations available through a straightforward process. In the UK, new subscription rules are due to take effect in spring 2027, introducing requirements that include a 14-day cooling-off period in certain circumstances, reminder notices, and the ability to cancel through the same channel used to sign up.


And these aren’t just theoretical risks. Noom agreed to[pay $56 million in cash and provide $6 million in subscription credits](https://journals.law.unc.edu/ncjolt/blogs/diet-app-noom-agrees-to-pay-56-million-to-settle-class-suit/) to settle a class action involving allegations of deceptive trial sign-ups, problematic cancellation practices, and unauthorized charges.


## Conclusion: should you move to web pricing?


We’ve covered a lot. And before making a decision, I suggest you go back to look at the comparison table at the top.


Don’t move to the web purely for the pricing opportunities or to avoid the 30% fee. Do it because you see an opportunity to reach your audiences there, build funnels that suit them, and experiment with pricing in ways you couldn’t before.


It’s easy to look at freelance life through rose-tinted glasses and forget that a good chunk of your time isn’t actually spent doing what you love, which in my case is growing apps. It’s spent dealing with the 40 other admin tasks that come with running your own business.


I learned that the hard way. Like when I started worrying that one client might not pay, and I didn't have legal insurance yet. (Luckily, they did pay in the end.) Even then, it took me a good half-day of research just to understand the options and get everything sorted. The extra freedom comes with extra costs and extra jobs, and moving to the web can feel much the same.


I wish someone had walked me through the accountant, the pension, the insurance, and everything else before I took the leap into freelancing. So consider this guide that walkthrough, for pricing on the web. When you’re ready to run your first pricing test on the web, **start with my[guide to web-to-app funnels](https://www.revenuecat.com/blog/growth/web-to-app-funnels) .**
